docs.title: TF-QKD / FSO Quantum Communication Framework
docs.text:
A research-oriented implementation framework for studying Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution (TF-QKD) and its potential deployment over Free-Space Optical (FSO) communication channels.

This project is being developed by Anand Kumar, B.Tech Electronics and Communication Engineering, under the guidance of Prof. Neelkanth Kundu (Indian Institute of Technology Delhi), with academic supervision and support from Prof. Yugnanda Malhotra.

The framework combines theoretical foundations, security analysis, channel modelling, literature review, and simulation-based investigations into a unified research environment for quantum communication studies.

docs.title: Project Objectives
docs.text:
The framework aims to:

  • Study the principles and security foundations of TF-QKD
  • Implement and validate key protocol components through simulation
  • Investigate secret-key generation under realistic channel conditions
  • Explore deterministic FSO channel models as an extension toward free-space quantum communication
  • Build a reproducible research platform for future protocol development and experimentation

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
Technical notes, derivations, implementation details, and conceptual explanations developed throughout the project.

Topics include:

  • TF-QKD fundamentals
  • Security proofs and assumptions
  • Channel transmittance modelling
  • Phase-error estimation
  • Secret-key rate analysis

docs.title: Literature Review
docs.text:
Curated collection of foundational and survey papers relevant to:

  • Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution
  • Quantum communication security
  • Free-space optical quantum channels
  • Satellite-based quantum networking

docs.title: Simulation Framework
docs.text: Phase Focus Area Phase 1 Foundations and Channel Modelling Phase 1 Extension Deterministic FSO Channel Modelling Phase 2 Cat-State Representation and Phase Error Analysis Phase 3 Key-Rate Optimization and Robustness Studies Phase 4 Finite-Decoy Linear Programming

docs.title: Research Vision
docs.text: The long-term objective of this work is to contribute toward practical and scalable quantum communication systems through rigorous modelling, simulation, and protocol analysis, with particular interest in long-distance and free-space quantum key distribution networks.

docs.title: Research Notebooks
docs.text: This section documents the implementation roadmap of the Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution (TF-QKD) research framework. The notebooks progress from protocol foundations and security analysis to practical finite-decoy implementations. An additional Free-Space Optical (FSO) extension investigates the deployment of TF-QKD over atmospheric channels.

docs.title: Foundation and Channel Model
docs.text: Introduces the theoretical foundations of Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution (TF-QKD), including protocol assumptions, optical losses, detector models, channel transmittance calculations, and baseline simulation infrastructure. This phase establishes the mathematical and computational framework used throughout the project.

docs.title: Phase 2 – Quantum States and Security Analysis
Cat States and Phase Error Analysis
docs.text: Implements the quantum-state representation employed in TF-QKD and studies phase-error estimation techniques required for security analysis. The notebook investigates the relationship between observable quantities and the security parameters governing secret-key generation.

docs.title: Phase 3 – Key Rate Optimization and Robustness
Key Rate Optimization and Robustness
docs.text: Explores parameter optimization strategies for maximizing secret-key rates under realistic operating conditions. Sensitivity analyses are performed to evaluate protocol robustness against channel loss, detector imperfections, and environmental disturbances.

docs.title: Finite Decoy Linear Programming
docs.text: Implements finite-decoy-state estimation using linear-programming methods. This phase transitions from idealized theoretical assumptions to experimentally realistic scenarios, enabling practical secret-key-rate evaluation with finite data samples.

docs.title: Extension Module – Free-Space Optical (FSO) Quantum Channels
Phase 1 Extension – Deterministic FSO Channel Modelling
FSO Channel
docs.text:
This notebook extends the Phase 1 channel modelling framework to free-space optical (FSO) communication links. The implementation focuses on deterministic propagation effects, including geometric beam spreading, atmospheric attenuation, link-budget calculations, and receiver coupling losses.

The objective is to establish a baseline FSO channel model before introducing stochastic effects such as turbulence-induced fading, scintillation, beam wander, or pointing errors in future developments.

Key topics include:

  • Free-space path loss
  • Atmospheric attenuation
  • Beam divergence effects
  • Receiver aperture collection efficiency
  • End-to-end channel transmittance
  • Deterministic link-budget analysis

This extension provides the foundational channel model required for future TF-QKD over FSO investigations and satellite-based quantum communication studies.

docs.title: Repository Resources
docs.text:
The repository also contains:

  • TF-QKD security-proof references
  • Technical documentation and project reports

Together, these materials form a comprehensive research framework for studying Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution and its potential deployment in advanced quantum communication networks.

docs.title: Simple Security Proof of Twin-Field Type Quantum Key Distribution Protocol
docs.text: Authors: Marcos Curty, Koji Azuma, Hoi-Kwong Lo Year: 2018 Author of Notes: Anand Ambastha

docs.title: Paper Information
docs.text:
This paper is one of the foundational theoretical works in Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution (TF-QKD).

Main contribution:

  • Simplified security proof for TF-QKD
  • Removes global phase matching requirement
  • Uses local phase randomization
  • Achieves square-root scaling:

$$ R \propto \sqrt{\eta} $$

instead of conventional:

$$ R \propto \eta $$

where:

  • (R) = secret key rate
  • (\eta) = channel transmittance

docs.title: Why This Paper Matters
docs.text:
Before this work:

  • TF-QKD security proofs were complicated
  • Existing proofs required global phase post-selection
  • Secret key rate reduced significantly
  • Experimental implementation became difficult

This paper simplified both:

  • theoretical analysis
  • practical implementation assumptions

Feels like this is one of the papers that pushed TF-QKD from just theory hype into something people could seriously work on experimentally.

docs.title: Background Motivation
docs.text:
Conventional QKD suffers from exponential loss in optical fibers.

For standard repeaterless QKD:

$$ R \propto \eta $$

Meaning key rate decreases linearly with channel transmittance.

TF-QKD changes this scaling using:

  • single-photon interference
  • middle measurement station
  • twin-field interference

Result:

$$ R \propto \sqrt{\eta} $$

This is the major breakthrough.

The paper also connects TF-QKD ideas with:

  • quantum repeaters
  • entanglement generation protocols
  • single-photon interference schemes

That conceptual connection is important.

docs.title: Main Idea of TF-QKD
docs.text:
Alice and Bob send weak optical states to a middle node Charlie.

Charlie performs interference measurement.

Security comes from:

  • interference statistics
  • decoy-state estimation
  • phase-error estimation

Unlike standard MDI-QKD:

  • only one effective photon arrival is needed
  • not two-photon coincidence detection

This is why scaling improves.

docs.title: Protocol 1 — Entanglement Based Version
docs.text: The paper first introduces an ideal entanglement-based protocol.

docs.title: State Preparation
docs.text:
Alice prepares:

$$ |\phi_q\rangle_{Aa} ===================

\sqrt{q}|0\rangle_A|0\rangle_a + \sqrt{1-q}|1\rangle_A|1\rangle_a $$

Bob prepares similar state.

Where:

  • (|0\rangle) = vacuum state
  • (|1\rangle) = single-photon state

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text: Alice and Bob prepare entangled optical states.

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text: Signals are sent to central node Charlie.

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Charlie applies:

  • 50:50 beamsplitter
  • threshold detectors

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text: Charlie announces detector click events.

docs.title: Step 5
docs.text:
Alice and Bob measure in:

  • X basis
  • Z basis

docs.title: Step 6
docs.text: Raw key extracted from detector outcomes.

docs.title: Important Observation
docs.text:
No global phase randomization is required.

This is one of the biggest simplifications compared to earlier TF-QKD approaches.

Global phase matching was experimentally painful.

Removing it improves practicality significantly.

docs.title: Detection Probabilities
docs.text:
The paper derives probabilities:

$$ r = r_1 + r_2 $$

where:

  • (r_1) = single-photon contribution
  • (r_2) = two-photon contribution

Single-photon interference is the key resource responsible for improved scaling.

docs.title: Error Rates
docs.text: Two important error rates:

docs.title: Phase Error Rate
docs.text:
$$ e_Z $$

The paper derives:

$$ 2e_X = e_Z $$

This relation becomes central to the security proof.

docs.title: Key Rate Formula
docs.text:
The asymptotic secret key rate:

$$ R_X ===

2r$$1-h(e_X)-h(e_Z)$$ $$

where:

  • (h(x)) = binary entropy function
  • (r) = success probability

Important because:

  • both bit errors and phase errors reduce key rate
  • phase-error estimation is the difficult part

docs.title: Protocol 2 — Prepare and Measure Version
docs.text:
The paper converts the entanglement-based protocol into a practical prepare-and-measure version.

This is important because practical systems do not generate ideal entangled states.

Prepared states:

docs.title: X Basis States
docs.text:
$$ |X_0\rangle = [\sqrt{q}|0\rangle + \sqrt{1-q}|1\rangle] $$

$$ |X_1\rangle = [ \sqrt{q}|0\rangle + \sqrt{1-q}|1\rangle] $$

docs.title: Z Basis States
docs.text:
$$ |Z_0\rangle = |0\rangle $$

$$ |Z_1\rangle = |1\rangle $$

docs.title: Practical Interpretation
docs.text:
This conversion is useful because:

  • easier implementation
  • closer to real optical systems
  • compatible with coherent pulse generation

docs.title: Protocol 3 — Practical TF-QKD
docs.text:
This is the practically relevant protocol.

Uses:

  • coherent states
  • decoy states
  • phase-randomized pulses
  • weak coherent pulses

docs.title: Signal States
docs.text:
Key generation states:

$$ |\alpha\rangle $$

and

$$ |-\alpha\rangle $$

These are coherent states.

docs.title: Decoy States
docs.text:
Decoy states are:

  • phase randomized coherent states
  • used for photon-number estimation
  • used for phase-error estimation

This enables decoy-state analysis.

docs.title: Decoy-State Method
docs.text:
The paper uses the idea that phase-randomized coherent states can be represented as mixtures of number states:

$$ P_\lambda(n)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!} $$

This allows Alice and Bob to estimate:

$$ p_{ZZ}(k_c,k_d|n_A,n_B) $$

Meaning:

probability of detector outcomes conditioned on photon numbers.

This is essential for security.

docs.title: Cat States in Security Proof
docs.text:
The paper introduces cat states:

$$ |C_0\rangle $$

and

$$ |C_1\rangle $$

These states are used for:

  • phase-error estimation
  • bounding Eve's information

This part is actually pretty nice mathematically.

docs.title: Most Important Security Equation
docs.text:
Upper bound on phase error:

$$ e_Z \le e_Z^{upp} $$

This equation is one of the core results of the paper.

Once phase error is bounded:

  • secret key rate becomes computable
  • security follows using entropy arguments

docs.title: PLOB Bound Discussion
docs.text:
The paper discusses beating repeaterless capacity limits.

PLOB bound states fundamental repeaterless rate-loss limit.

Simulation results in the paper show:

  • TF-QKD surpassing PLOB bound
  • even with realistic detector imperfections

This is probably one of the main reasons TF-QKD exploded as a research area.

docs.title: Important Experimental Assumptions
docs.text:
The paper assumes:

  • synchronized phase references
  • stable interference visibility
  • coherent state generation
  • decoy-state estimation

These assumptions look simple theoretically.

Practically they are difficult.

docs.title: 1. Phase Stabilization
docs.text:
Very difficult experimentally.

Especially over long fiber distances.

Problems:

  • thermal drift
  • laser linewidth mismatch
  • fiber vibration
  • environmental noise

docs.title: 2. Dark Counts
docs.text:
At long distances:

  • signal becomes weak
  • detector dark counts dominate

This can increase QBER rapidly.

docs.title: 3. Mode Matching
docs.text:
Single-photon interference requires:

  • temporal matching
  • spectral matching
  • polarization matching

Even small mismatch reduces visibility.

docs.title: 1. Simpler Security Proof
docs.text:
Compared to earlier TF-QKD security analyses:

  • much cleaner
  • more elegant
  • easier to interpret physically

docs.title: 2. Removal of Global Phase Matching
docs.text:
Big practical improvement.

Probably one of the strongest parts of the paper.

docs.title: 3. Strong Conceptual Foundation
docs.text:
Paper clearly connects TF-QKD with:

  • entanglement generation
  • quantum repeaters
  • single-photon interference physics

This gives strong physical intuition.

docs.title: 4. Better Key Rate Performance
docs.text:
Paper claims significant improvement over earlier TF-QKD proofs.

Likely correct under asymptotic assumptions.

docs.title: 1. Asymptotic Analysis
docs.text:
Major limitation.

Paper assumes:

  • infinite signals
  • infinite decoy states
  • perfect statistics

Real systems cannot achieve this.

Finite-key analysis is missing.

docs.title: 2. Practical Complexity Still High
docs.text:
Although simplified theoretically:

experimental TF-QKD is still hard.

Especially:

  • phase stabilization
  • long-distance interference
  • synchronization

docs.title: 3. Security Still Relies on Ideal Models
docs.text:
Security proof still assumes:

  • idealized detectors
  • ideal state preparation
  • simplified noise models

Real systems contain more imperfections.

docs.title: 4. Dark Count Sensitivity
docs.text:
Long-distance operation remains vulnerable to:

  • detector noise
  • finite visibility
  • weak signal levels

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: $$ R \propto \sqrt{\eta} $$

docs.title: Conventional QKD Scaling
docs.text: $$ R \propto \eta $$

docs.title: Key Rate Equation
docs.text: $$ R_X = 2r \left[1 - h(e_X) - h(e_Z)\right] $$

docs.title: Phase Error Bound
docs.text: $$ e_Z \le e_Z^{upp} $$

docs.title: Research Importance
docs.text:
This paper strongly influenced later TF-QKD protocols including:

  • PM-QKD
  • SNS-TF-QKD
  • no-phase-postselection TF-QKD
  • practical decoy-state TF systems

Many later papers are extensions or refinements of this framework.

docs.title: Finite-Key TF-QKD
docs.text: Still major open problem.

docs.title: Satellite TF-QKD
docs.text:
Very difficult because of:

  • turbulence
  • Doppler shift
  • free-space phase instability

But potentially revolutionary.

docs.title: Integrated Photonic TF-QKD
docs.text: Important for commercialization.

docs.title: Machine Learning Assisted Stabilization
docs.text:
Could help with:

  • adaptive phase correction
  • drift prediction
  • real-time optimization

Interesting future direction.

docs.title: Overall Thoughts
docs.text:
This paper honestly feels like one of the core TF-QKD papers.

A lot of later papers are basically extending ideas from here.

Not perfect obviously, but definitely important.

Things I found important:

  • simpler security proof
  • more practical than earlier TF-QKD versions
  • gives physical intuition properly
  • validates square-root scaling

Main problems:

  • asymptotic assumptions are unrealistic
  • experimental implementation still hard
  • phase stabilization is still painful

But those are mostly field-wide TF-QKD problems rather than failures unique to this paper.

docs.title: Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution: Protocols, Security, and Open Problems
docs.text: Authors: Syed M. Arslan, Syed Shahmir, Noureldin Mohammad, Saif Al-Kuwari, Muataz Alhussein Year: 2025 Author of Notes: Anand Ambastha

docs.title: Paper Overview
docs.text:
This is a survey paper on Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution (TF-QKD).

The paper mainly covers:

  • TF-QKD basics
  • protocol variants
  • security proofs
  • experimental demonstrations
  • practical implementation problems
  • open research directions

This is not a protocol invention paper.

It is more like a large literature consolidation paper for TF-QKD.

docs.title: Main Motivation
docs.text:
The survey repeatedly explains why TF-QKD became important.

Main reason:

Conventional repeaterless QKD scales as:

[ R \propto \eta ]

while TF-QKD can achieve:

[ R \propto \sqrt{\eta} ]

This scaling improvement is the central theme of the entire paper.

docs.title: Why TF-QKD Matters According to Paper
docs.text:
The survey explains that TF-QKD:

  • extends communication distance
  • can surpass PLOB bound
  • avoids trusted repeaters
  • supports future quantum networks

The paper positions TF-QKD as an important candidate for:

  • intercity quantum communication
  • long-distance secure fiber links
  • future quantum internet infrastructure

docs.title: Historical Flow Discussed in Paper
docs.text: The survey gives a timeline-like progression:

docs.title: BB84
docs.text:
First major QKD protocol.

Uses non-orthogonal quantum states.

docs.title: Decoy State QKD
docs.text:
Introduced to fight:

  • photon-number splitting attacks

Uses intensity variation.

docs.title: MDI-QKD
docs.text:
Introduced to remove detector-side attacks.

Uses untrusted middle measurement node.

docs.title: TF-QKD
docs.text:
Extends MDI ideas.

Uses:

  • single-photon interference
  • coherent state interference
  • middle node detection

Result:

improved scaling.

docs.title: Important TF-QKD Variants Covered
docs.text: The survey discusses several protocol families.

docs.title: 1. Original TF-QKD
docs.text:
Based on Lucamarini proposal.

Uses:

  • weak coherent pulses
  • phase encoding
  • central interference measurement

Main issue:

phase stabilization difficulty.

docs.title: 2. PM-QKD (Phase Matching QKD)
docs.text:
Uses phase matching between Alice and Bob.

Advantages:

  • high distance performance
  • strong theoretical framework

Problems:

  • phase post-selection complexity
  • experimental difficulty

docs.title: 3. SNS-TF-QKD (Sending-or-Not-Sending)
docs.text:
One of the most important practical TF-QKD variants.

Main idea:

Alice/Bob randomly decide:

  • send pulse
  • not send pulse

Advantages:

  • better robustness against errors
  • strong long-distance performance
  • practical improvements

This protocol family became very popular experimentally.

docs.title: 4. No-Phase-Postselection Variants
docs.text:
Attempt to reduce complexity caused by:

  • global phase matching
  • heavy post-selection

Important because phase post-selection reduces key rate.

docs.title: Security Discussion
docs.text:
One thing I liked:

The paper actually discusses practical attacks instead of pretending QKD is magically secure.

docs.title: 1. MITM Attacks
docs.text:
Survey correctly points out:

QKD without authentication is vulnerable.

This is something many beginners misunderstand.

Quantum mechanics alone does NOT solve authentication.

docs.title: 2. Photon Number Splitting (PNS)
docs.text:
Survey explains:

  • weak coherent pulses contain multi-photon components
  • Eve can exploit this
  • decoy-state method is used as countermeasure

docs.title: 3. Trojan Horse Attacks
docs.text:
Attacker injects bright light into system.

Goal:

extract internal modulation information.

Paper discusses:

  • optical isolators
  • monitoring detectors
  • filtering

as countermeasures.

docs.title: 4. Detector Blinding Attacks
docs.text:
APDs can be forced into classical regime using strong light.

Then Eve can manipulate clicks.

Survey correctly mentions:

MDI-QKD helps solve detector-side vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 5. Time Shift Attacks
docs.text:
Uses detector efficiency mismatch.

Attacker manipulates photon arrival timing.

Countermeasures include:

  • synchronization
  • detector equalization
  • MDI approaches

docs.title: Important Point About Security
docs.text:
The paper repeatedly mentions that:

practical security is different from ideal theoretical security.

This is actually a good point.

Real systems always contain:

  • imperfections
  • side channels
  • detector issues
  • source leakage

docs.title: Experimental Discussion
docs.text:
The survey discusses:

  • long-distance fiber demonstrations
  • stabilization systems
  • interference visibility
  • detector technologies

The paper mentions distances beyond:

  • 500 km

for some TF-QKD demonstrations.

docs.title: 1. Phase Stabilization
docs.text:
Probably biggest issue in TF-QKD.

Need stable interference between:

  • independent lasers
  • long-distance channels

Very difficult practically.

docs.title: 2. Fiber Drift
docs.text:
Environmental changes cause:

  • phase drift
  • polarization fluctuation
  • visibility degradation

docs.title: 3. Detector Noise
docs.text:
Dark counts become dangerous at large distance.

Especially because TF-QKD often depends on single-click events.

docs.title: 4. Synchronization
docs.text:
Need accurate:

  • timing synchronization
  • frequency matching
  • phase locking

for stable interference.

docs.title: Finite-Key Discussion
docs.text:
The survey mentions finite-key analysis multiple times.

This is important because:

real systems do NOT operate in asymptotic conditions.

Real experiments have:

  • finite pulses
  • finite statistics
  • imperfect estimation

The survey says this is still an open problem in many TF-QKD variants.

docs.title: Network Discussion
docs.text:
The survey also discusses:

  • SDN integration
  • metropolitan quantum networks
  • multi-user systems
  • future quantum internet

Honestly these sections feel more future-looking than practically mature.

Still useful for understanding research direction.

docs.title: Table II
docs.text:
Compares existing TF-QKD survey papers.

Actually useful.

Shows:

  • which surveys cover experiments
  • which cover security
  • which discuss implementations

The paper claims broader coverage than earlier surveys.

docs.title: Publication Trend Figures
docs.text:
Survey shows TF-QKD publication growth over years.

Interesting observation:

research activity increased rapidly after:

  • PLOB bound discussions
  • early TF-QKD demonstrations

This matches actual trend in literature.

docs.title: What I Found Good in This Survey
1. Broad Coverage
docs.text:
Covers:

  • protocols
  • security
  • experiments
  • networking
  • implementation

Useful for literature review.

docs.title: 2. Honest About Challenges
docs.text:
The paper does not pretend TF-QKD is solved completely.

Clearly mentions:

  • finite-key issues
  • stabilization problems
  • practical deployment difficulty

Good sign.

docs.title: 3. Security Discussion Better Than Many Surveys
docs.text:
At least discusses:

  • detector attacks
  • Trojan horse attacks
  • PNS attacks
  • authentication problems

Many survey papers completely ignore practical attacks.

docs.title: 4. Nice Historical Structure
docs.text:
The BB84 → MDI → TF-QKD progression is explained clearly.

Good for beginners entering quantum communication.

docs.title: 1. Too Broad Sometimes
docs.text:
The paper tries covering:

  • history
  • security
  • networking
  • experiments
  • implementation
  • protocols
  • future internet

Result:

some sections become shallow.

Especially:

  • finite-key mathematics
  • composable security proofs
  • experimental DSP techniques

could have been deeper.

docs.title: 2. Limited Mathematical Depth
docs.text:
This is not a highly mathematical survey.

Many derivations are discussed conceptually.

Not ideal if someone wants:

  • full proofs
  • detailed derivations
  • implementation mathematics

docs.title: 3. Engineering Discussion Could Be Better
docs.text:
The survey mentions stabilization issues.

But practical details like:

  • optical PLLs
  • FPGA synchronization
  • linewidth tolerance
  • active feedback systems

are not deeply analyzed.

docs.title: 4. Some Sections Feel Descriptive
docs.text:
At places it feels more like:

"listing papers and summarizing them"

instead of critically synthesizing results.

Still useful though.

docs.title: Finite-Key TF-QKD
docs.text: Still major issue.

docs.title: Real-World Stabilization
docs.text: Probably largest practical bottleneck.

docs.title: Multi-User TF-QKD
docs.text: Interesting future direction.

docs.title: Quantum Network Integration
docs.text:
Still early-stage.

Especially coexistence with classical telecom traffic.

docs.title: Satellite TF-QKD
docs.text:
Potentially huge research area.

But technically extremely difficult.

docs.title: My Personal Observations
docs.text:
This paper is useful mainly as:

  • literature review source
  • roadmap paper
  • beginner-to-intermediate TF-QKD reference

Not the best paper for:

  • deriving protocols
  • implementing systems directly
  • advanced mathematical security proofs

docs.title: Overall Thoughts
docs.text:
Good survey paper overall.

Not revolutionary research.

But definitely useful.

Strongest parts:

  • broad TF-QKD coverage
  • organized structure
  • practical security discussion
  • comparison of variants

Main weaknesses:

  • not mathematically deep enough
  • some sections feel descriptive
  • engineering analysis could be stronger
  • finite-key discussion still limited

Still a solid reference paper for someone entering TF-QKD research.
